title: The Caliph Hisham and the Arab Youth

keywords: the caliph hisham and the arab youth
full_text:
The Umayyad Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik rode out hunting across the northern steppes of Syria with a splendid retinue of emirs, falconers, and palace guards. While pursuing a desert gazelle, the Caliph became separated from his escort and rode near an isolated well where a young Bedouin boy was watering his flock of sheep.

The Caliph’s stallion was thirsty, and Hisham called out with imperious authority: 'Ho, boy! Draw water for the horse of the Commander of the Faithful!'

The Bedouin boy looked up with untroubled eyes, his head held high: 'Your stallion may drink when my sheep have finished, O traveler. The beasts of the poor have thirsted all day under the sun, and the water of the earth belongs equally to all living creatures.'

Hisham frowned, his pride wounded: 'Do you know to whom you speak with such bold speech, insolent child? I am Hisham, the ruler of all the Faithful from Morocco to Samarkand!'

The boy smiled with calm dignity and replied: 'If you are indeed the shepherd of the people, O Caliph, remember that a true shepherd watches over the weakest lamb before he feeds his own horse. Power is a trust from the heavens, not a rod to strike down the humble.'

Hisham was astonished by the youth’s fearlessness and the philosophical depth of his reply. At that moment, the royal guards galloped up, drawing their swords to punish the boy for his lack of deference.

'Hold your hands!' commanded Hisham. 'This desert child has taught your Caliph more wisdom in three breaths than all the flatterers in my court have spoken in twenty years.' The Caliph dismounted, embraced the boy, rewarded his tribe with five hundred sheep and a fertile oasis, and took the youth to his capital to be trained in the highest councils of the realm.
moral: Inborn eloquence and sharp intellect outshine royal power and command respect from emperors.
